title: Prepositions and their cases

objectives.can: Say which case a preposition is governing and how the case changes its sense.

explanation.summary: A Greek preposition stands before a noun or pronoun and 'governs' it: the noun must be in a case that the preposition allows. Some prepositions take one case only. Others take two or three, and then the case changes the meaning.

sections.heading: Preposition plus case
body: A prepositional phrase is a preposition, its noun (often with an article) and any adjective that goes with the noun: ἐν ἀρχῇ in John 1:1, πρὸς τὸν θεόν in the same verse. The preposition itself never changes its form. What it does is demand a case. In πρὸς τὸν θεόν the article and the noun are accusative; in ἐν ἀρχῇ the noun is dative.

English has only prepositions, so 'in', 'into', 'out of' and 'from' are separate words. Greek splits the work between the preposition and the case. This is why you must always read the case of the noun after a preposition: the same preposition can mean different things with different cases.

sections.heading: Prepositions with one case
body: A few common prepositions take only one case in the New Testament. ἐν is followed by the dative: 'in, among, by'. εἰς is followed by the accusative: 'into, to, for', as in εἰς τὸν κόσμον in John 3:17. ἐκ and ἀπό are followed by the genitive: 'out of' and 'from', as in ἀπὸ θεοῦ in 1 Corinthians 1:3. πρό ('before') takes the genitive and σύν ('with') the dative, as in σὺν Χριστῷ in Philippians 1:23.

Because ἐν and εἰς look so alike, remember the pairing: ἐν takes the dative (where something is), εἰς takes the accusative (where something goes). ἐκ and ἀπό both mean 'from', but ἐκ is 'out of' and ἀπό 'away from'.

sections.heading: Prepositions with two or three cases
body: Many of the commonest prepositions take more than one case, and the case changes the sense. A good first rule is that the genitive often points to separation, source or agent, the accusative often to direction, extent or aim, and the dative often to position or accompaniment. The table below sets out the commonest meanings; it is a first guide, not a complete list.

For example, διά with the genitive means 'through' (δι’ αὐτοῦ, 'through him', John 1:3), and with the accusative 'because of' (διὰ τὸν λόγον, John 15:3). μετά with the genitive means 'with' (μετ’ ἐμοῦ), and with the accusative 'after' (μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἓξ, Matthew 17:1). κατά with the genitive often means 'against' (κατ’ ἐμοῦ), and with the accusative 'according to' (κατὰ τὰς γραφάς, 1 Corinthians 15:3).

ἐπί, παρά and πρός are less simple. ἐπί takes the genitive, dative or accusative with senses such as 'on', 'upon', 'over', 'at' and 'to'; παρά takes all three with the sense of 'beside' or 'from beside'; πρός is nearly always followed by the accusative in the New Testament and means 'to, towards' or 'with', as in πρὸς τὸν θεόν.

sections.heading: Elision
body: When a preposition ends in a vowel and the next word begins with a vowel, the final vowel is usually dropped and an apostrophe is written: δι’ αὐτοῦ for διὰ αὐτοῦ, ἀπ’ for ἀπό, μετ’ for μετά. If the next word begins with a rough breathing, the consonant before the apostrophe is aspirated: μεθ’ ἡμέρας, ἐφ’, ἀφ’, καθ’. The elided form is the same word, with the same case rule; to find the preposition in a lexicon, undo the elision.

sections.heading: How to read a prepositional phrase
body: Find the preposition. Find the noun after it (past the article, if there is one) and read its case. Then choose the sense of the preposition that fits that case and the verb. Often one or two senses will be possible, and the verb and the rest of the clause will decide.

misunderstandings: The preposition does not change the noun after it. It selects which case that noun must be in, and the case was already there in the ending.
A preposition has no single English equivalent. ἐν is usually 'in', but it can also be 'among', 'by' or 'with', depending on the noun. Learn the common senses, not one gloss.
Do not translate by the case alone. The genitive does not always mean 'of' after a preposition, and the accusative does not always mean 'to'; the preposition and the case work together.
The apostrophe in δι’, ἀπ’, μετ’ is not a different word. It shows a dropped vowel.

deeper.heading: Cases and the older language
body: In earlier Greek, the cases did most of the work that prepositions do now, and the prepositions were adverbs that made the sense of a case clearer. By the New Testament, prepositions have become far more frequent, and some cases are used less on their own. A well-known trend is that εἰς overlaps with ἐν in some places, and a few grammarians read this as a sign of the change; others are more cautious, so be careful about deciding on meaning from this alone.

examples.analysis: Two prepositional phrases. ἐν takes the dative: ἐν ἀρχῇ, 'in the beginning' (the noun is dative singular). πρός takes the accusative: πρὸς τὸν θεόν, 'with God', literally 'towards' God, the article and noun both accusative.

reading.why: The prologue of John is full of short prepositional phrases: ἐν, πρός, διά, χωρίς, περί, εἰς. You can find the preposition, the case and the sense in each.
